## Design

### 2026-10-06 – spent about 6 hours working on buddy's week 1 pcb design.

**6h**

spent about 6 hours working on buddy's week 1 pcb design.

i started by figuring out what buddy actually needs from its main board and chose the esp32-s3-wroom-1-n16r8 as the brain. i also decided to use the devkit version with headers so the board is realistic for me to assemble as a beginner.

then i worked through the main hardware for buddy, including the display, audio amp and speaker, motor driver and motors, tof distance sensor, power system, buttons, rgb led, and expansion headers. i also removed some features like the microphone, imu, and wheel encoders for now so the board doesn't become unnecessarily complicated.

after that, i researched specific parts and made the initial bom with actual products, prices, and vendors. the estimated parts cost came out to around $84–91.

i then made the final pin map for the esp32-s3 and assigned pins for the display, audio, motors, tof sensor, buttons, and rgb led. i also checked which pins needed to stay unused because of psram, usb, or other special functions.

most of the time was spent researching and checking  that the parts and pin assignments would actually work together before starting the schematic. no pcb has been routed yet.

### 2026-10-08 – figured out what lives on the PCB vs what plugs in. everything swappable: DevKitC on two female header sockets, all four breakout modules on male headers, motors and speaker on screw terminals. 11 con

**3h**

figured out what lives on the PCB vs what plugs in. everything swappable: DevKitC on two female header sockets, all four breakout modules on male headers, motors and speaker on screw terminals. 11 connectors, 93 pins total.

went through the full parts list and added all the connectors — female headers, screw terminals, motor brackets. total came out to $73.16 across Amazon, Adafruit, SparkFun, and Digi-Key.

blocked out the power zone first: USB screw terminal → PTC fuse → rocker switch in a straight line. high-current path is short and easy to inspect. switch mounts through the chassis wall.

placed the two 1×19 female sockets for the DevKitC centered on the board. it dominates the real estate - everything else fans out from the GPIO columns.

matched each breakout header to its GPIO side: J_AMP near I²S pins, J_TOF near I²C, J_DISP near SPI2, J_MOTOR near PWM. short traces, low noise.

C1 1000µF bulk cap within 10mm of the motor driver VM pin. output screw terminals along the bottom edge so wires exit the chassis cleanly. buttons and LED along the top edge to poke through the panel.

board fully zoned at 80×70mm. fits the JLCPCB $2 tier with room to spare. next is KiCad entry and the autorouter.

### 2026-10-08 – placed every component on the 80×70mm board today. started with the power zone — USB terminal into the fuse into the rocker switch, straight line top-left. high current, short path, easy to probe.

**5h**

placed every component on the 80×70mm board today. started with the power zone — USB terminal into the fuse into the rocker switch, straight line top-left. high current, short path, easy to probe.

the DevKitC sockets went center board. two 1×19 female headers, 51mm tall. once those were locked in, everything else had to fan out from the GPIO columns — not much freedom there, which is actually fine because it keeps traces short.

matched each breakout header to the GPIO side it talks to. amp near the I²S pins, ToF near I²C, display near SPI2, motor driver near PWM. one side per bus. screw terminals for motors and speaker along the bottom so wires drop straight out the chassis floor.

passives cluster on the right — C1 1000µF bulk cap within 10mm of the motor driver VM pin. buttons and RGB LED poking up through the top panel.

board fully zoned. 80×70mm, fits the JLCPCB $2 tier. total BOM landed at $73.16 across one Amazon order, one Adafruit, one SparkFun, one Digi-Key.
